question: Adenosine is effective for terminating AV node-dependent re-entry tachycardias (AVNRT, AVRT) because it transiently hyperpolarises the AV node by activating GIRK channels, interrupting the re-entry circuit — but it is ineffective and potentially dangerous in atrial flutter or ventricular tachycardia.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. Adenosine terminates SVTs that use the AV node as part of their re-entry circuit (AVNRT, AVRT). It is not effective for atrial flutter (circuit is entirely atrial) and is ineffective/dangerous in most VTs. Its very short half-life (~10 seconds) limits systemic side effects.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Adenosine acts on A1 receptors on the AV node → Gi protein → activates GIRK (IKAch) channels → hyperpolarisation → AV block (transient). This terminates AVNRT/AVRT (which require AV conduction). In atrial flutter, adenosine may transiently unmask flutter waves (diagnostic) but does not terminate it. In VT (without AV node involvement in the circuit), adenosine is generally ineffective and can cause haemodynamic deterioration.
